title: Centripetal vs Centrifugal Force
assumptions: Ideal horizontal top-down view with no air resistance or vertical gravity effects.
Mass is constant and the string is massless and inextensible.
The rotating frame rotates at a constant angular velocity omega.
Diagrams are schematic and not to scale unless specified by the numerical graph.

scenes.title: Why Does It Fly Out?
scenes.goal: Pose the core question: why does an object seem to fly outward when released from circular motion?
motion: A cyan ball moves in a circle on a dark navy background.
A red arrow points inward, labeled 'Net Force'.
The string snaps, and the ball flies off in a straight line tangent to the circle.
A ghost trail shows the path the ball would have taken if it stayed in the circle.
scenes.caption: When the string breaks, the ball flies straight, not outward. Why?
physics_checks: Velocity vector is tangent to the circle at the moment of release.
Net force vector is radial and inward before release.
Post-release trajectory is a straight line tangent to the circle.

scenes.title: Velocity and Acceleration Directions
scenes.goal: Establish that in uniform circular motion, velocity is tangent and acceleration/net force is inward.
motion: Cyan ball moves in a circle with a green velocity vector tangent to the path.
A red net force vector points radially inward toward the center.
A dashed line connects the ball to the center, labeled 'radius r'.
The ball completes two full rotations, with the vectors updating continuously.
scenes.caption: Velocity is tangent. Net force and acceleration point inward.
physics_checks: Green velocity vector is always perpendicular to the radius vector.
Red net force vector is always parallel to the radius vector and points inward.
The magnitude of the velocity vector remains constant.

scenes.title: Tangent Release Path
scenes.goal: Demonstrate that upon release, the object follows the instantaneous tangent at constant speed.
motion: The ball moves in a circle with a visible trail.
At a specific point, the string visually breaks.
The ball continues in a straight line along the tangent.
A second, ghost ball continues the circular path to contrast the two trajectories.
scenes.caption: No outward force. The ball follows the tangent at constant speed.
physics_checks: The release point is clearly marked.
The straight-line path is exactly tangent to the circle at the release point.
The speed of the released ball matches the tangential speed at release.

scenes.title: Force Depends on Speed Squared
scenes.goal: Show the relationship F_net = m*v^2/r using a live numerical graph.
motion: A cyan ball moves in a circle with a red inward force vector.
A live graph appears on the right, plotting Force (y-axis) vs Speed (x-axis).
As the ball's speed increases, the red force vector lengthens.
Data points appear on the graph: (2, 2), (4, 8), (6, 18) for m=1kg, r=2m.
A curve F = v^2/2 is drawn through the points.
scenes.caption: Doubling speed quadruples the required inward force. F = m*v^2/r.
physics_checks: The graph axes are labeled 'Speed (m/s)' and 'Force (N)'.
The plotted points correspond to v=2,4,6 m/s and F=2,8,18 N.
The red force vector length is proportional to the calculated force.

scenes.title: Inertial vs Rotating Frames
scenes.goal: Compare the view from an inertial frame and a rotating frame, introducing centrifugal force.
motion: Split screen: left side shows inertial frame, right side shows rotating frame.
In the inertial frame, the ball moves in a circle with an inward red force.
In the rotating frame, the ball appears stationary.
An amber arrow points outward from the ball in the rotating frame, labeled 'Centrifugal Force'.
The amber arrow balances the red inward force in the rotating frame view.
scenes.caption: In a rotating frame, a fictitious outward force balances the inward force.
physics_checks: The rotating frame background rotates at a constant angular speed omega.
The ball is stationary relative to the rotating frame background.
The amber centrifugal force vector is radially outward.
The magnitude of the amber force equals the magnitude of the red force.

scenes.title: Left-Turning Car Physics
scenes.goal: Apply the concepts to a car turning left, distinguishing real forces from fictitious ones.
motion: Top-down view of a car turning left on a curved road.
A red friction force vector points inward on the car.
A passenger (cyan dot) is shown inside the car.
As the car turns, the passenger slides toward the right door (tangent path).
The door exerts an inward contact force on the passenger, shown as a red arrow.
An amber centrifugal force arrow is shown on the passenger in the car's rotating frame.
scenes.caption: Friction turns the car. The door pushes the passenger inward.
physics_checks: The car's path is a left turn (curving to the left).
The friction force on the car is inward (toward the center of the turn).
The passenger's initial motion is tangent to the turn.
The contact force from the door on the passenger is inward.

scenes.title: Real vs Fictitious Forces
scenes.goal: Summarize the difference between centripetal (real net force) and centrifugal (fictitious) forces.
motion: Two side-by-side diagrams: left for inertial frame, right for rotating frame.
In the inertial frame, a red inward arrow is labeled 'Centripetal (Net Force)'.
In the rotating frame, a red inward arrow and an amber outward arrow are shown.
The amber arrow is labeled 'Centrifugal (Fictitious)'.
Text appears: 'Centripetal: Real interaction. Centrifugal: Frame-dependent effect.'
scenes.caption: Centripetal is a real net force. Centrifugal is a frame-dependent effect.
physics_checks: The red arrow in the inertial frame is labeled as a net force.
The amber arrow in the rotating frame is labeled as fictitious.
The directions of the forces are correctly depicted (inward vs outward).
